_meta.title: Which Bracha? — flowchart data
_meta.note: MIXED CONTENT, two source works. (1) Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi's Shulchan Aruch HaRav, Orach Chaim (via Chabad.org, Eliyahu Touger/Sholom B. Wineberg translation), at 'core rulings only' depth: siman 202 (cat_tree_fruit branch), siman 203 (cat_ground_produce branch), siman 204 (meat/fish/dairy/eggs default, general food-spoilage downgrade rule, water-only-blessed-when-thirsty rule, extra wine detail folded into final_hagafen), siman 205 (vegetables raw-vs-cooked, veggie juice/cooking-water), siman 207 (bracha achrona — Borei Nefashot text and when it applies), and siman 212 (ikar/tafel — mixed foods: grain supremacy, dominant/majority-component rule, accompaniment case). Simanim 206, 213, 214, and 215 (interruptions/errors, holding food in the right hand, doubt-resolution defaults, equinox/dangerous-water customs, fulfilling another's obligation, the 'Baruch...Melech ha'olam' formula, answering Amen) were reviewed but are mechanics/procedure rather than which-bracha-to-say logic, so none were built into branches. Simanim 208-231 do not survive in the Alter Rebbe's original Shulchan Aruch text (confirmed repeatedly by 'not extant' footnotes) — this is why bread/mezonot and the Me'ein Shalosh after-blessings (Al Hamichyah/Al Hagefen/Al Ha'etz) couldn't be sourced from the Shulchan Aruch HaRav alone. (2) The Alter Rebbe's own Seder Birkas HaNehenin (via Chabad.org, same translators) now fills that gap: ch. 2 ('The Detailed Laws Governing the Blessing Over Bread', 15 halachos) is fully built into the bread/mezonot branch (cat_bread, cat_mezonot, bread_meal_context, bread_filling_check, boiled_then_baked_check, final_hamotzi, final_mezonot, final_mezonot_fried, final_mezonot_boiled) — covering plain bread, thin crackers (trisa), enriched/soft dough with its meal-quantity upgrade rule, savory- vs. sweet-filled pastries, fried dough, and boiled/cooked dough (including the boiled-then-baked-restores-Hamotzi rule). Remaining PLACEHOLDER CONTENT: the exact text of Al Hamichyah/Al Hagefen/Al Ha'etz (Me'ein Shalosh) was referenced by name throughout ch. 2 but never quoted verbatim there — expected in ch. 7 ('Details Concerning the Blessings Recited over Other Foods and Beverages'), not yet reviewed. Birkat Hamazon's full liturgical text is intentionally not reproduced (out of scope, like simanim 206/213-215) — only its triggering conditions are sourced. 12 of 14 supplied Seder Birkas HaNehenin files (overview + ch. 1, 3-13) remain unreviewed as of this pass; only ch. 2 has been processed so far. Minor edge-case machloket intentionally omitted throughout, consistent with the rest of this app's scope. Explanations are written in plain, layman-friendly language; fuller technical/halachic reasoning is kept in each source's footnote 'note' field. Nodes carry "placeholder": false once genuinely sourced; "placeholder": true and the literal string PLACEHOLDER/PENDING still mark content awaiting real source text. Do not treat placeholder content as halachically authoritative. Citations for Shulchan Aruch HaRav content are siman:seif; for Seder Birkas HaNehenin content, chapter:halacha. "link" fields are left empty until a specific chabad.org/Sefaria URL can be confirmed rather than guessed.

start.question: What are you eating or drinking?

options.label: Bread
Mezonot / grain product (cake, pastry, pasta, cereal, etc.)
Fruit
Vegetable
Wine or grape juice
Other drinks (water, soda, coffee, tea, non-grape juice)
Meat, fish, dairy, or eggs
A mixture of multiple food types
Food that's spoiled, stale, or gone downhill
options.label_he: אוכל שהתקלקל, התיישן, או ירד מאיכותו

options.label: Plain water
A flavored drink (soda, coffee, tea, juice, etc.)
options.label_he: משקה בטעם (סודה, קפה, תה, מיץ, וכו')

sources.note: Plain water only gives a person enjoyment when they're thirsty — so it's the one beverage where the blessing depends on why you're drinking it. Other beverages give enjoyment through their flavor regardless of thirst, so they always get a blessing.

water_thirst_check.question: Are you drinking because you're thirsty, or just to wash something down (like a pill, or food stuck in your throat)?
water_thirst_check.question_he: האם אתה שותה כי אתה צמא, או רק כדי להעביר משהו (כמו כדור, או אוכל שנתקע בגרון)?

options.label: I'm thirsty
Just washing something down, not thirsty
options.label_he: רק כדי להעביר משהו, לא צמא

sources.note: No blessing — before or after — is said over water drunk only to swallow a pill or dislodge food, since there's no enjoyment in it; the person isn't drinking for the water itself.

spoiled_food_check.question: Is it still edible at all, even in a pinch — or is it completely inedible now?
spoiled_food_check.question_he: האם זה עדיין ראוי לאכילה ולו בדוחק — או שזה כבר לגמרי לא ראוי לאכילה?

options.label: Still edible, even if it's gone downhill
options.label_he: עדיין ראוי לאכילה, גם אם ירד באיכותו

options.label: Completely inedible, even in a pinch
options.label_he: לגמרי לא ראוי לאכילה, אפילו בדוחק

sources.note: Whenever food's quality has deteriorated (its examples: bread gone a bit moldy, a cooked dish whose look and quality declined), its blessing downgrades from whatever specific bracha it would normally get to the generic Shehakol. If it has spoiled entirely — not fit to eat even under pressing circumstances — no blessing at all is said, the same as fully moldy bread.

cat_bread.question: Is this a plain bread-style item — a loaf, roll, bagel, or pita made from just flour and water, kneaded into a firm dough and baked in an oven?
cat_bread.question_he: האם זהו פת פשוטה - כיכר, לחמניה, בייגל או פיתה, העשויה מקמח ומים בלבד, שנילושה לבצק מוצק ונאפתה בתנור?

options.label: Yes, plain flour-and-water bread
No — it's enriched, thin, filled, fried, or boiled/cooked
options.label_he: לא - זה מועשר, דק, ממולא, מטוגן, או מבושל

sources.note: Plain bread — of the kind people normally base a meal on, made from flour kneaded with water into a firm dough and baked — always takes Hamotzi and triggers Birkat Hamazon once at least a k'zayit (~28.8cc/1 fl. oz.) has been eaten, regardless of whether you're actually full. This differs from breads/baked goods that aren't "standard" — those only get Hamotzi if eaten in a meal-sized quantity (see following questions).

bread_meal_context.question: Are you eating enough of it that it's serving as your actual meal — roughly the amount of bread most people would eat at breakfast or dinner (not just a snack or small amount)?
bread_meal_context.question_he: האם אתה אוכל כמות כזו שהיא משמשת כסעודה ממש - בערך הכמות שרוב האנשים אוכלים בארוחת בוקר או ערב (ולא רק חטיף או כמות קטנה)?

options.label: Yes, this is my meal
No, just a snack/small amount
options.label_he: לא, רק חטיף או כמות קטנה

sources.note: There are many opinions on the exact minimum amount. The Alter Rebbe's practical guidance: eating an amount equal to roughly four egg-sized portions or more of these breads, to the point of being satisfied, upgrades the blessing to Hamotzi and Birkat Hamazon (recited over this food alone). Eating less than that, or not being satisfied even after eating a large amount, keeps the blessing at Mezonot / Al Hamichyah.

cat_mezonot.question: What kind of item is it, and how was it made?
cat_mezonot.question_he: מהו סוג הפריט, וכיצד הוא הוכן?

options.label: A cracker, wafer, thin flatbread, or crispy snack — thin and crisp all the way through, even after baking
options.label_he: קרקר, וופל, פת דקה, או חטיף פריך - דק ופריך לגמרי, גם אחרי האפייה

options.label: A soft roll, bun, cake, or sweet bread — made with milk, juice, honey, oil, wine, or eggs (not just flour and water), or a soft dough that isn't full firm bread-dough
options.label_he: לחמניה רכה, עוגה, או לחם מתוק - העשוי מחלב, מיץ, דבש, שמן, יין או ביצים (לא רק קמח ומים), או בצק רך שאינו בצק לחם מוצק

options.label: A pastry with a filling baked inside it (filled before baking)
options.label_he: מאפה עם מילוי אפוי בתוכו (שממולא לפני האפייה)

options.label: Fried in oil (like a donut or fried dough)
options.label_he: מטוגן בשמן (כמו סופגנייה או בצק מטוגן)

options.label: Boiled or cooked in water/soup/a pot (like a dumpling or kreplach)

sources.note: The Alter Rebbe classifies baked/cooked grain products into these categories. Thin/crispy items (trisa) never upgrade to Hamotzi no matter how much you eat. Soft/enriched breads and fillings can upgrade to Hamotzi if eaten as a full meal-sized portion. Fried and boiled/cooked dough generally stay Mezonot regardless of quantity, with some further distinctions covered in the following questions.

options.label: The fruit itself
Juice from the fruit
Water it was cooked or soaked in
options.label_he: מים שבישלו או השרו בהם את הפרי

options.label: A leaf, stem, peel, or pit — not the fruit itself
options.label_he: עלה, גבעול, קליפה, או גרעין — לא הפרי עצמו

sources.note: Establishes that the bracha for fruit that grows on trees is Ha'etz, a distinct bracha from Ha'adama, precisely because of the fruit's own body/substance — which is why juice, cooking-water, and non-fruit parts of the tree are each analyzed separately below.

options.label: Yes, ripe
No, it's unripe or small
options.label_he: לא, הוא לא בשל או קטן

sources.note: The baseline rule (202:1) applies straightforwardly to ripe fruit; 202:4 addresses fruit picked before it has finished ripening.

tree_fruit_edible_check.question: Can you eat it at all right now?

options.label: Yes, it's edible
No, it's inedible (too bitter, sour, or hard)
options.label_he: לא, אי אפשר לאכול אותו (מר, חמוץ, או קשה מדי)

sources.note: As long as fruit that has emerged is not so bitter/sour that it's unfit to eat even under pressing circumstances, it already has the halachic status of 'fruit' and gets Ha'etz, even if very small.

tree_fruit_sweetened_check.question: Was it sweetened or cooked to make it edible?
tree_fruit_sweetened_check.question_he: האם הוא הומתק או בושל כדי להפוך אותו לאכיל?

options.label: Yes
No, still inedible

sources.note: Fruit inedible even under pressing circumstances gets no bracha at all when eaten as-is; if it is later sweetened by fire or another means, since it was never fit to eat without that intervention, it is not treated as returning to full fruit status — the bracha is Shehakol, not Ha'etz.

tree_fruit_juice_type.question: What kind of juice is it?

options.label: Wine or grape juice
Olive oil
Any other fruit juice

sources.note: Squeezed fruit juice is generally not considered the body of the fruit and gets Shehakol — even juice that oozes out on its own, like date-honey. Grapes and olives are the sole exceptions: what emerges from them is legally 'the fruit itself,' since pressing them to produce wine and oil is the primary reason those trees are planted. Wine is nonetheless removed from Ha'etz into its own bracha (Hagafen) because of its importance; oil, though logically warranting Ha'etz, is not given a blessing at all when drunk plain (since it is harmful and not enjoyed that way) — only when mixed with another beverage for genuine enjoyment.

Confirms the same rule in the Alter Rebbe's later work: squeezed fruit juice takes Shehakol, not the fruit's own blessing — except juice from olives and grapes, which keeps the fruit's status (though wine still gets its own dedicated bracha, Hagafen, due to its importance, and oil is handled separately — see final_oil_complex).

tree_fruit_ancillary_intent.question: Do people normally eat this part too, not just the fruit?
tree_fruit_ancillary_intent.question_he: האם רגילים לאכול גם חלק זה, ולא רק את הפרי?

options.label: Yes (like caper leaves)
No (like a palm tree's inner core)

sources.note: Any growth on a tree that is not the primary fruit is not important enough for Ha'etz. It gets Ha'adama if the tree is planted with the intent that this growth be eaten too (its example: caper leaves and shoots); otherwise it is not tied to the purpose of the planting at all and gets Shehakol (its example: the date palm's edible heart/crown, and vine twigs).

cat_ground_produce.question: Does it grow on a plant that lives for years, or does it grow back fresh from the ground every year — even if it looks tree-like (like a banana or pineapple plant)?
cat_ground_produce.question_he: האם זה גדל על צמח שחי שנים רבות, או שזה צומח מחדש מהאדמה בכל שנה — גם אם זה נראה כמו עץ (כמו בננה או אננס)?

options.label: Lives for years, like a tree
Grows back fresh every year, or it's a regular vegetable
options.label_he: צומח מחדש בכל שנה, או שזה ירק רגיל

sources.note: Defines the test for tree-fruit vs. ground-produce: if the branch a fruit grew on survives the winter and bears fruit again the next year, it's tree fruit (Ha'etz). If the plant dies back entirely and regrows fresh from the root each year, its produce is Ha'adama — even if it looks tree-like. (Later authorities apply this to explain why bananas and pineapples, for example, get Ha'adama.)

ground_produce_type.question: Is it a root or a spice — something that grows underground, or is mainly used as a seasoning?
ground_produce_type.question_he: האם זה שורש או תבלין — משהו שגדל מתחת לאדמה, או משמש בעיקר כתבלין?

options.label: No, it's a regular vegetable, leaf, or produce
options.label_he: לא, זהו ירק רגיל, עלה, או תוצרת

options.label: Yes, a root, spice, or seasoning
Raw
Cooked or pickled
Juice squeezed from it
Water it was cooked in

sources.note: The blessing Ha'adama is recited over vegetables whether eaten raw or cooked. This also applies to kitniyos suitable either way. Even vegetables most people only eat together with bread (its example: onions), still get Ha'adama when eaten alone.

veggie_raw_common_check.question: Do people commonly eat this particular vegetable raw too — not just cooked?
veggie_raw_common_check.question_he: האם רגילים לאכול ירק זה גם חי — ולא רק מבושל?

options.label: Yes
No — it's normally only eaten cooked or pickled (like cabbage, squash, or a dried field bean)
options.label_he: לא — בדרך כלל נאכל רק מבושל או כבוש (כמו כרוב, דלעת, או קטנית יבשה מהשדה)

sources.note: Even if a vegetable is more palatable cooked, if most people also eat it raw, the blessing Ha'adama is recited on it raw too.

Vegetables people don't normally eat raw at all (its examples: cabbage, squash, spinach) get Shehakol raw and Ha'adama once cooked or pickled. The same applies to dried kitniyos (beans/legumes) grown in a field to be dried and cooked — eating them raw, even fresh, is Shehakol; only kitniyos grown in a garden specifically to be eaten raw (and their pods) get Ha'adama raw.

ground_produce_spice_check.question: Do people ever eat it on its own — even prepared, like candied ginger, or roasted as a home remedy — or is it only ever used to flavor other food?
ground_produce_spice_check.question_he: האם אי פעם אוכלים אותו לבד — גם אם מוכן, כמו זנגביל מסוכר, או קלוי כתרופה ביתית — או שהוא משמש רק לתיבול מאכל אחר?

options.label: Yes, sometimes eaten on its own
No, only ever used to flavor other food
options.label_he: לא, משמש רק לתיבול מאכל אחר

sources.note: Spices/roots commonly eaten on their own once prepared (its examples: ginger, peppercorns, cloves) get Ha'adama even when honey or sugar is what made them edible, since the honey/sugar is secondary. Spices people never eat by themselves and use only to season cooked food (its example: saffron) never attain the status of produce at all — even if made edible on its own for a curative purpose, they still get Shehakol, because they weren't grown with the intent of being eaten themselves.

mixed_start.question: Are these foods truly mixed or combined together (like a stew, trail mix, or a filled pastry) — or are you eating two separate foods side by side (like bread alongside something salty)?
mixed_start.question_he: האם המאכלים באמת מעורבים או משולבים יחד (כמו תבשיל, תערובת אגוזים, או בצק ממולא) — או שאתה אוכל שני מאכלים נפרדים זה לצד זה (כמו פת לצד משהו מלוח)?

options.label: Mixed or combined together
Separate foods, eaten side by side
options.label_he: מאכלים נפרדים, נאכלים זה לצד זה

sources.note: The primary-covers-secondary principle applies whether the two foods are physically mixed together, prepared with the intent to be eaten together (like a dough filled with fruit), or simply eaten side by side where one food is eaten only because of the other.

mixed_grain_check.question: Does it contain an actual grain product (bread, pasta, cereal, a pastry crust) that you intend to actually eat — not just a trace of flour used to thicken something?
mixed_grain_check.question_he: האם יש בו מוצר דגן ממשי (לחם, פסטה, דגנים, בצק) שאתה מתכוון לאכול בפועל — ולא רק שביב קמח לסמיכות?

options.label: Yes, real grain, and I want to eat it
options.label_he: כן, דגן ממשי, ואני רוצה לאכול אותו

options.label: No — no real grain, or it's just a trace/coating
options.label_he: לא — אין דגן ממשי, או שזה רק שכבה דקה

sources.note: Whenever the actual substance of a grain product (not just its flavor) is part of a mixture, it's considered primary (ikar) and takes precedence over everything else in the mixture — even if it's only a small amount — as long as you actually intend to eat it and not just use it as a wrapper or thickener that's dissolved into liquid.

mixed_dominant_check.question: Is one part clearly the main reason you're eating this — with everything else there just to accompany, flavor, or improve it — or does one part simply make up most of the mixture?
mixed_dominant_check.question_he: האם חלק אחד הוא הסיבה העיקרית לאכילה — והשאר רק מלווה, מתבל, או משפר אותו — או שחלק אחד מהווה את רוב התערובת?

options.label: Yes, one part is clearly dominant
No — a few parts feel roughly equally important to me
options.label_he: לא — כמה חלקים חשובים לי באותה מידה בערך

sources.note: One recites the blessing over the food of primary importance (ikar) and it covers the food of secondary importance (tafel) — both for the blessing before eating and the one after. This applies whether the secondary food is mixed in only to improve/enable the primary food, or the two foods are simply unequal in amount (the larger portion being primary), or they were prepared with intent to be eaten together (e.g. a dough filled with fruit) even if not physically mixed.

mixed_accompaniment_check.question: Are you eating the second food only to help you get through the first — like bread to protect your throat from something salty, or to offset a strong drink — and you wouldn't be eating it right now otherwise?
mixed_accompaniment_check.question_he: האם אתה אוכל את המאכל השני רק כדי לעזור לך עם הראשון — כמו פת להגן על הגרון ממאכל מלוח, או לרכך משקה חזק — ולא היית אוכל אותו עכשיו בלעדיו?

options.label: Yes, purely to help with the first — I don't want it for its own sake
options.label_he: כן, רק כדי לעזור עם הראשון — לא רוצה אותו בפני עצמו

options.label: No, I also want to eat it for its own sake
options.label_he: לא, אני גם רוצה לאכול אותו בפני עצמו

sources.note: Even when two foods aren't mixed together at all, if a person is primarily partaking of one and only partakes of the second because of the first — such that he would not partake of the second at all right now if not for the first — the second is considered auxiliary and is covered by the first's blessing. Its example: a person eats bread together with salted fish just so the fish won't harm his throat; the bread becomes secondary to the fish and is covered by the fish's Shehakol. This applies only when the person is not hungry and has no desire at all for the secondary food on its own — if he does want it too, even eaten together with the primary food, it needs its own blessing (Hamotzi, for bread), since food commonly served as part of a meal is always covered by the bread's own blessing regardless.

final_mixed_dominant.bracha_name: Say the bracha for the dominant part — it covers the rest
final_mixed_dominant.bracha_name_he: אמור את הברכה על החלק הדומיננטי — הוא פוטר את השאר
final_mixed_dominant.explanation: Find that dominant ingredient's own bracha by walking through this tool again for that specific food (Fruit / Vegetable / etc.) — then say only that one blessing. It covers everything else mixed in or eaten alongside it, even parts that would otherwise need a different bracha of their own.

sources.note: The blessing over food of primary importance covers food of secondary importance, both for the blessing before and after eating.

final_mixed_equal.bracha_name: Say a separate bracha for each different type
final_mixed_equal.bracha_name_he: אמור ברכה נפרדת לכל סוג שונה
final_mixed_equal.explanation: When no single part is really dominant, the general approach is to say the right bracha for each different type of food separately, walking through this tool for each one. (There's normally a preferred order for which bracha to say first when several apply — that source, siman 211, isn't available in this tool yet.)

sources.citation: Shulchan Aruch HaRav, Orach Chaim 212, translator's note 39
sources.note: Example given: a fruit salad made of some fruits needing Ha'etz and others needing Ha'adama, with no single fruit forming the majority — both blessings are said, each over a piece of the relevant fruit. The rule governing which blessing takes precedence when several apply lives in siman 211, which is not extant in the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch.

final_mixed_accompaniment_secondary.bracha_name: No separate bracha needed — the first food's blessing covers it
final_mixed_accompaniment_secondary.bracha_name_he: אין צורך בברכה נפרדת — ברכת המאכל הראשון פוטרת אותו
final_mixed_accompaniment_secondary.explanation: Since you wouldn't be eating this at all right now if not for the other food, it's "secondary" — you skip its own blessing, and the primary food's blessing already covers it. This holds even if the secondary food would normally need a more specific bracha of its own, like bread's Hamotzi — as long as you genuinely have no appetite for it on its own.

sources.note: Its example: eating bread together with salted fish purely so the fish won't harm the throat — the bread is secondary to the fish and covered by the fish's Shehakol, even though bread is normally the most prestigious food and would otherwise need its own Hamotzi.

final_mixed_accompaniment_own.explanation: Since you want to eat it for its own sake too — not only to help you get through the other food — it needs its own bracha, even though you're eating the two together. Find its bracha by walking through this tool for that specific food.

sources.note: If a person also desires to partake of the (in the source's example) bread, even eating it together with the salted food, it is not secondary to the salted food, even if he desires the salted food more. He must recite the blessing appropriate to the food he also wants for itself.

final_hamotzi.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.
final_hamotzi.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם הַמּוֹצִיא לֶחֶם מִן הָאָרֶץ
final_hamotzi.explanation: Bread eaten as/with a meal takes the bracha of Hamotzi, which — per the halachic principle of 'ikar v'tafel' — covers other foods eaten as part of that meal. Plain flour-and-water bread is always Hamotzi, even for a small amount (a k'zayit). Non-standard baked goods (enriched dough, filled pastry with a savory filling, or dough that was boiled/cooked and then baked or dry pan-fried) also reach full Hamotzi status — either automatically (savory fillings) or once eaten as a genuine meal-sized portion.

sources.note: Plain bread of the kind people normally base a meal on always takes Hamotzi and Birkat Hamazon once a k'zayit is eaten, regardless of satisfaction.
Non-standard breads (enriched dough, thicker soft rolls) upgrade to Hamotzi once eaten as a genuine meal-sized portion — practically, about four egg-sized portions or more, eaten to satisfaction.

A pastry filled with savory, meal-type food (meat, fish, cheese, or vegetables) keeps full Hamotzi status even for a k'zayit, regardless of quantity, since such a filling doesn't remove the dough from the halachic category of bread.
Dough that was cooked/boiled and then baked in an oven or fried in a pan without much liquid has its bread status fully restored, even in pieces smaller than a k'zayit.

bracha_achrona.name: Birkat Hamazon (Grace After Meals)
bracha_achrona.text_en: The full, multi-paragraph Grace after Meals (four blessings), recited from a bencher or siddur — not reproduced here, as it's a long liturgical text rather than a short bracha. It's required once at least a k'zayit (~28.8cc/1 fl. oz.) of bread has been eaten; Scripturally, the obligation is triggered by eating to the point of satisfaction, but the Sages extended it to apply to a k'zayit even without being full.
bracha_achrona.text_he: [הנוסח המלא אינו מובא כאן — נמצא בסידור/בנצ'ר]

sources.note: Scripturally, Birkat Hamazon is only required after eating bread to the point of satisfaction; the Sages ordained it be recited even after just a k'zayit.

Explains that although the count of four separate blessings within Birkat Hamazon is a Rabbinic ordinance, Moshe Rabbeinu himself instituted the wording of the first blessing (Birkat Hazan) as its own self-contained blessing — which is why a doubt about the obligation is treated stringently, similar to a Scriptural-level doubt.

final_mezonot.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates various kinds of sustenance.
final_mezonot.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי מְזוֹנוֹת
final_mezonot.explanation: Grain-based baked goods that aren't standard, plain, meal-staple bread — crackers/thin crisp items, or enriched/soft breads and sweet-filled pastries eaten in less than a full meal-sized portion — take the bracha of Mezonot rather than Hamotzi.

sources.note: Thin, crispy baked goods (trisa) never get Hamotzi, however much is eaten, since they never reach the halachic appearance of bread.
Dough enriched with milk, fruit juice, or other liquids besides water is generally Mezonot; a meticulous person is stringent and eats it only after already reciting Hamotzi on plain bread.
Non-standard breads stay at Mezonot unless eaten as a genuine meal-sized portion (roughly four egg-sized portions or more, to the point of satisfaction).

bracha_achrona.name: Al Hamichyah (Me'ein Shalosh)
bracha_achrona.text_en: [PENDING — Seder Birkas HaNehenin ch. 2 and ch. 7 (both reviewed) reference this blessing by name dozens of times but never quote its text verbatim, unlike short one-line brachot (Shehakol, Ha'etz, Hagafen) which do get quoted in full. This appears to be a consistent pattern in this source: it's a halachic/legal text, not a siddur, so it doesn't reproduce longer prayer texts. bracha_achrona.text_he: [ממתין — הנוסח המדויק לא הופיע בפרקים ב' ו-ז'; ככל הנראה יש להביאו מסידור/בנצ'ר]

Both Seder Birkas HaNehenin ch. 2 (bread laws) and ch. 7 (other foods/beverages) reference this blessing extensively but never quote its text — likely because it's a longer liturgical text, similar to how Birkat Hamazon's text isn't reproduced either. final_haetz.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who created the fruit of the tree.
final_haetz.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ
final_haetz.explanation: Fruit that grows on trees gets its own blessing, Ha'etz — that's the standard bracha for any tree fruit.

sources.note: The opening ruling of the chapter: the bracha for all fruit that grows on trees (whether one of the seven species Eretz Yisrael is praised for, or any other species) is Ha'etz. Although the fruit is ultimately nourished from the earth, the Sages gave tree fruit its own distinct bracha because of its importance.

bracha_achrona.name: Borei Nefashot — unless this fruit is one of the five fruits among the shivat haminim (grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, dates), which get a different after-blessing instead
bracha_achrona.name_he: בורא נפשות — אלא אם כן זהו אחד מחמשת הפירות משבעת המינים (ענבים, תאנים, רימונים, זיתים, תמרים), שיש להם ברכה אחרונה אחרת
bracha_achrona.text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates many souls and their needs, for everything You have created to sustain the life of every living thing. Blessed is the Life of all worlds.
bracha_achrona.text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא נְפָשׁוֹת רַבּוֹת וְחֶסְרוֹנָן עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָאתָ לְהַחֲיוֹת בָּהֶם נֶפֶשׁ כָּל חָי בָּרוּךְ חֵי הָעוֹלָמִים

sources.note: Borei Nefashot is the after-blessing for tree fruit, "with the exception of those from the five species" — grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives, and dates, the five fruits among the shivat haminim (the seven species Eretz Yisrael is praised for). Those five instead get "the one blessing that encapsulates three" (Al Ha'etz / Me'ein Shalosh) — that text lives in siman 208, which is not extant in the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch, so it isn't sourced in this app yet. Applies once at least a k'zayit (~28.8cc/1 fl. oz.) has been eaten.

final_haetz_unripe.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ
final_haetz_unripe.explanation: Even unripe fruit still counts as fruit, as long as you can eat it — so it still gets Ha'etz, just like ripe fruit.

sources.note: As soon as a tree produces fruit, even very small and not yet ripe, it already has the status of "fruit" and takes Ha'etz — as long as it isn't so bitter or sour that it's unfit to eat even in a pinch.
This leniency is limited to fruit still developing on the tree when picked — not to withered/scorched fruit, or fruit whose season passed without ripening, which instead gets Shehakol.

final_shehakol_sweetened_fruit.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, by whose word everything came to be.
final_shehakol_sweetened_fruit.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיָה בִּדְבָרוֹ
final_shehakol_sweetened_fruit.explanation: This fruit wasn't edible at all on its own — it only became edible once it was sweetened or cooked. Since it never counted as real fruit to begin with, it gets the everyday blessing, Shehakol, instead of Ha'etz.

sources.note: Fruit inedible even under pressing circumstances is never considered halachic "produce" at all — it's treated as mere wood. Even after it's later sweetened by fire, honey, or another means and becomes edible, it doesn't regain Ha'etz status, because it was never fit to eat without that intervention.

bracha_achrona.text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates many souls and their needs, for everything You have created to sustain the life of every living thing. Blessed is the Life of all worlds.
bracha_achrona.text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא נְפָשׁוֹת רַבּוֹת וְחֶסְרוֹנָן עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָאתָ לְהַחֲיוֹת בָּהֶם נֶפֶשׁ כָּל חָי בָּרוּךְ חֵי הָעוֹלָמִים

final_no_bracha.explanation: This isn't edible at all right now, and hasn't been fixed up to become edible. Since there's nothing to actually enjoy eating, no blessing is said.

sources.note: On fruit specifically: "Provided it is not so bitter or sour that it is unfit to be eaten, even in a pressing situation. In the latter instance, no blessing should be recited over it at all."
The general version of the same rule for any food: if it has spoiled entirely — not fit to eat even under pressing circumstances — no blessing at all is said, e.g. bread that has gone fully moldy.

final_no_bracha_water.explanation: Plain water only gives real enjoyment when you're actually thirsty. If you're just using it to wash down a pill or dislodge food, there's no enjoyment in the water itself — so no blessing is said, before or after.

sources.note: "The blessing Shehakol nih'yah bidvaro should not be recited before drinking water, nor the blessing Borei nefashos afterwards, unless one drinks because he is thirsty. If, however, one drinks to swallow a cheekful [of food] that is causing him to choke, he should not recite a blessing, neither beforehand nor afterwards." (Other beverages always get a blessing regardless of thirst, since their flavor itself is enjoyable.)

final_shehakol_spoiled.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, by whose word everything came to be.
final_shehakol_spoiled.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיָה בִּדְבָרוֹ
final_shehakol_spoiled.explanation: Once food's quality has gone downhill, it drops out of whatever specific blessing it would normally get and falls back to the everyday catch-all blessing, Shehakol.

sources.note: "Whenever the quality of a food has deteriorated, e.g., bread became somewhat moldy or the appearance of food changed and deteriorated slightly, its blessing is downgraded [from] the specific blessing designated for it. [Instead,] the general blessing that includes all foods — Shehakol nih'yah bidvaro — is recited over it."

final_shehakol_cooking_water.explanation: Even though the water picked up the fruit's flavor, the water itself isn't the fruit — so drinking it on its own gets the everyday blessing, Shehakol.

final_oil_complex.explanation: Plain oil isn't pleasant to drink, so by itself it gets no blessing at all. Mainly for the other drink or food, and the oil's just along for the ride (e.g. oil mixed into beer, or eaten with bread) → say that drink's/food's own blessing instead, which covers the oil.

sources.note: Olives are planted specifically to produce oil, so oil is legally "the fruit itself" and in principle deserves Ha'etz — but plain oil is harmful and gives no enjoyment, so no blessing is said over it by itself. Once mixed with another beverage for genuine enjoyment, the bracha follows whichever element (oil or the other beverage) is the primary reason for drinking — full ikar/tafel analysis of intent and proportion is in the source.

Gives concrete examples: oil eaten with bread, or mixed into beer (as was common) — the bread/beer is primary, and its own blessing covers the oil. Exception: someone with a sore throat who drinks oil mixed with other beverages specifically to heal it — the oil counts as primary despite being the smaller part, since that's their actual intent, so Ha'etz is said and covers the other beverages.

final_haadama_ancillary.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who created the fruit of the ground.
final_haadama_ancillary.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה
final_haadama_ancillary.explanation: This isn't the tree's main fruit, but it's still something people normally eat — so it counts as regular produce and gets Ha'adama.

final_haadama.explanation: Vegetables, roots, and other produce that grows fresh from the ground each year get this everyday blessing.

bracha_achrona.name: Borei Nefashot
bracha_achrona.text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates many souls and their needs, for everything You have created to sustain the life of every living thing. Blessed is the Life of all worlds.
bracha_achrona.text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא נְפָשׁוֹת רַבּוֹת וְחֶסְרוֹנָן עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁבָּרָאתָ לְהַחֲיוֹת בָּהֶם נֶפֶשׁ כָּל חָי בָּרוּךְ חֵי הָעוֹלָמִים

sources.note: Borei Nefashot is recited after: tree fruit (other than the five fruits among the shivat haminim / seven species, which get a different after-blessing — see siman 208, not extant in the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch), ground produce, leafy vegetables, and any food that doesn't grow from the earth at all (meat, dairy, etc.) — provided at least a k'zayit (an olive's-bulk, roughly 28.8cc/1 fl. oz.) was eaten. Eating several such foods together still only requires one Borei Nefashot, since they all share the same after-blessing. This blessing closes with "Baruch chei ha'olamim" rather than repeating Hashem's full name, unlike Birkat Hamazon.

final_shehakol_veggie_raw.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, by whose word everything came to be.
final_shehakol_veggie_raw.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיָה בִּדְבָרוֹ
final_shehakol_veggie_raw.explanation: This vegetable isn't normally eaten raw, so eating it raw isn't really "the way it's meant to be eaten" — it gets the everyday blessing instead. (Cooked or pickled, it goes back to Ha'adama.)

sources.note: Vegetables people don't normally eat raw, even with bread (its examples: cabbage, squash, spinach), get Shehakol raw and Ha'adama once cooked or pickled — including turnips and carrots, which get Ha'adama when cooked even if cooked without meat, since cooking with meat for flavor is simply their normal preparation.

Dried kitniyos (beans/legumes) eaten raw get Shehakol, since that's not their normal use — except garden beans grown specifically to be eaten raw, which get Ha'adama raw (including their pods). Kitniyos grown in a field to be dried and cooked stay Shehakol raw even while still fresh/moist.

sources.citation: Shulchan Aruch HaRav, Orach Chaim 205, footnote 8
sources.note: This category can shift with common practice: the Rebbe (Rabbi Menachem M. Schneerson), citing the Alter Rebbe's own Seder Birkas HaNehenin, notes the rule isn't fixed — it follows how people actually eat the vegetable at the time. Raw carrots, for example, are commonly eaten today, so they now get Ha'adama raw as well; later authorities (Piskei Teshuvos) extend this to raw cabbage too.

final_haadama_veggie_water.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who created the fruit of the ground.
final_haadama_veggie_water.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה
final_haadama_veggie_water.explanation: Unlike fruit-cooking water, water a vegetable was cooked in is treated the same as the vegetable itself — because people commonly plan to eat the broth along with (or instead of) the vegetable, so it never really leaves the category of food.

sources.note: "One should... recite the blessing Borei pri haadamah on the water in which [vegetables] are cooked" — in contrast to fruit-cooking water, which gets Shehakol (siman 202:11), because vegetables are typically planted with the intent that their broth be eaten too.

final_shehakol_flavoring.explanation: Some spices are never eaten as food on their own — only used to flavor other dishes. Since they were never grown to be eaten by themselves, they don't count as real produce, so they get the everyday blessing instead.

final_hagafen.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.
final_hagafen.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגָּפֶן
final_hagafen.explanation: Wine is important enough that it gets its own special blessing, Hagafen, instead of the regular fruit blessing. This still counts as wine even if it's been boiled, gone a bit sour (as long as people still call it wine), or has honey/spices mixed in. It stops counting as wine — dropping to Shehakol — if it's watered down enough that it's no longer recognizable or drunk as wine (a rough guide: about 1 part wine to 6 parts water), or if another beverage was mixed in heavily enough to spoil the wine's own taste.

sources.note: What emerges from grapes is legally "the fruit itself" (unlike ordinary fruit juice), since producing wine is the primary reason grapevines are planted — so on the underlying logic, wine would deserve Ha'etz. But because wine is important — it satiates and gladdens the heart — the Sages gave it its own bracha, Hagafen, instead. Reciting Ha'etz over wine does not fulfill the obligation.

Wine that smells like vinegar but still tastes like wine keeps its Hagafen status (taste, not smell, is what counts); if the taste itself has turned to vinegar, it's Shehakol. Boiled wine is not considered lesser-quality wine — its blessing doesn't change.

Honey or pepper mixed into wine doesn't change its blessing. Another beverage mixed in enough to spoil the wine's own taste drops it to Shehakol. Water mixed in keeps Hagafen as long as the result is still strong enough to be drunk and recognized as wine — roughly, up to about six parts water to one part wine; beyond that it's no longer considered wine at all.

Confirms and adds detail: wine diluted with water keeps Hagafen as long as it's still strong enough to be recognized and commonly drunk as wine at that dilution — an individual's personal willingness to call heavily-diluted wine "wine" doesn't count if most people wouldn't. Once water reaches six times the wine's volume, Hagafen is never said, regardless of strength or custom.

final_shehakol_drink.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, by whose word everything came to be.
final_shehakol_drink.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיָה בִּדְבָרוֹ
final_shehakol_drink.explanation: Fruit or vegetable juice (other than wine and, in its own special case, oil) just gets the everyday blessing, Shehakol — and so does any other flavored drink like soda, coffee, or tea.

sources.note: Squeezed fruit juice is not considered the body of the fruit — even if it oozed out on its own — so it takes Shehakol rather than Ha'etz, with wine and (in its own more complex way) olive oil as the exceptions.
Squeezed vegetable juice gets Shehakol just like other produce juice — even though, unlike juice, the water vegetables are cooked in gets Ha'adama.
Unlike plain water, other beverages give real enjoyment through their flavor, so they always get a blessing before and after drinking, regardless of whether the person is thirsty.

final_shehakol_other.explanation: Meat, fish, dairy, and eggs don't grow from the ground or a tree at all, so they get the everyday catch-all blessing, Shehakol — the same as mushrooms, since mushrooms feed off moisture in the air rather than truly growing from the earth.

sources.note: "The blessing Shehakol nih'yah bidvaro is recited on foods that do not grow from the earth" — its examples: meat of domesticated and wild animals, fowl, fish, milk, cheese, eggs, water, salt, and honey. Mushrooms and truffles are included too: although they grow from the earth, their nurture comes from moisture and the atmosphere rather than the earth itself (and they can grow on wood or utensils), so they're not considered "fruit of the earth."
Confirms the same rule in the Alter Rebbe's later work, using nearly identical wording.

bread_filling_check.question: Is the filling a savory, meal-type food (meat, fish, cheese, or vegetables) — or something sweet (fruit, nuts, honey, sugar)?
bread_filling_check.question_he: האם המילוי הוא מאכל מלוח מסוג ארוחה (בשר, דגים, גבינה, או ירקות) - או משהו מתוק (פירות, אגוזים, דבש, או סוכר)?

options.label: Savory — meat, fish, cheese, or vegetables
options.label_he: מלוח - בשר, דגים, גבינה, או ירקות

options.label: Sweet — fruit, nuts, honey, or sugar
options.label_he: מתוק - פירות, אגוזים, דבש, או סוכר

sources.note: A pastry filled with savory, meal-type food (meat, fish, cheese, or vegetables) keeps full bread status and gets Hamotzi even for just a k'zayit, since the filling doesn't remove the dough from the halachic category of bread. A pastry filled with sweets or fruit is treated as made for enjoyment rather than sustenance, so it stays at Mezonot unless eaten in a meal-sized quantity.

boiled_then_baked_check.question: After it was boiled or cooked, was it then also baked in an oven or pan-fried without much added liquid (for example, kreplach that get pan-fried afterward, or a baked kugel/casserole)?
boiled_then_baked_check.question_he: לאחר הבישול, האם זה גם נאפה בתנור או טוגן במחבת יבשה יחסית (לדוגמה קרעפלאך שמטגנים אחרי הבישול, או קוגל/תבשיל אפוי)?

options.label: Yes, baked or pan-fried afterward
options.label_he: כן, נאפה או טוגן לאחר מכן

options.label: No, it stayed boiled/cooked

sources.note: Dough cooked in a pot (boiled) is never considered bread, however much is eaten, and always takes Mezonot — even in large pieces. But if it's subsequently baked in an oven, or fried in a pan without much liquid, its bread status is fully restored and it takes Hamotzi, even in pieces smaller than a k'zayit.

final_mezonot_fried.bracha_text_en: Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who creates various kinds of sustenance.
final_mezonot_fried.bracha_text_he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה' אֱלֹקֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם בּוֹרֵא מִינֵי מְזוֹנוֹת
final_mezonot_fried.explanation: Dough that's fried in oil (donuts, fried dough, pan-fried dumplings) generally stays at Mezonot, even if you'd end up quite full from it — frying doesn't give it the same status as oven-baking. Still, if you plan to eat enough to be fully satisfied, proper practice is to only do so as part of an actual bread meal (i.e., after already saying Hamotzi on real bread), to avoid a doubt about whether Birkat Hamazon is required.

sources.note: Soft dough fried in liquid (like crepes/pancakes) never reaches bread status, however much is eaten — all authorities agree on this, since it was never a firm dough to begin with.

Thicker, bread-like dough that's fried in oil is disputed among the authorities; the Alter Rebbe rules that fundamentally, frying is treated like cooking (i.e., Mezonot) rather than baking — but out of deference to the stringent opinion, one who intends to eat to the point of satisfaction should do so only within a meal that includes real bread.

sources.note: Confirmed by Shulchan Aruch HaRav 207:1 that mezonot from the five grains gets "the one blessing that encapsulates three" (Al Hamichyah) instead of Borei Nefashot. Both Seder Birkas HaNehenin ch. 2 (bread laws) and ch. 7 (other foods/beverages) reference this blessing extensively but never quote its text — likely because it's a longer liturgical text, similar to how Birkat Hamazon's text isn't reproduced either. The exact wording will likely need to come from a siddur/bencher.
